questions.question: Which command creates a new empty Git repository in the current directory?
questions.explanation: git init creates the .git directory for a new repository.

questions.question: Which command stages changes to file.txt for the next commit?
questions.explanation: git add places the current content in the index (staging area).

questions.question: Which command shows which files are modified, staged or untracked?
questions.explanation: git status summarises the working tree and index state.

questions.question: Which command copies a remote repository into a new local directory?
questions.explanation: git clone creates a new local repository from a remote one.

questions.question: Which command creates a branch named feature and switches to it?
questions.explanation: git switch -c (like git checkout -b) creates and switches to a new branch.

questions.question: Which file lists patterns of untracked files Git should ignore?
questions.explanation: .gitignore patterns stop untracked files from being added or reported.

questions.question: Which command displays the commit history of the current branch?
questions.explanation: git log lists commits reachable from HEAD.

questions.question: Which command uploads your local branch's commits to the remote repository?
questions.explanation: git push updates remote refs with your local commits.

questions.question: How does git fetch differ from git pull?
options: fetch downloads commits and updates remote-tracking branches without changing your current branch
fetch also merges the changes into your branch
fetch deletes local branches that were removed remotely by default
questions.explanation: git pull is fetch followed by a merge (or rebase); fetch alone does not touch your branch.

questions.question: Which command unstages file.txt but keeps its changes in the working tree?
questions.explanation: restore --staged resets the index entry to HEAD and leaves the working copy alone.

questions.question: Which command temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch to other work?
questions.explanation: git stash saves local modifications and reverts to a clean working tree.

questions.question: What does git commit --amend do?
options: Adds a new commit after HEAD with the same message
Edits the commit before the last one
Replaces the last commit with a new one containing the staged changes and/or a new message
questions.explanation: --amend rewrites the tip commit, giving it a new hash.

questions.question: Which command creates a new commit that undoes the changes made by commit abc123?
questions.explanation: revert adds an inverse commit, which is safe on shared history.

questions.question: In a merge conflict, what do the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers separate?
options: Staged and unstaged versions of the file
Your current branch's version and the incoming branch's version
The local and the stashed versions
The first and last commits of the branch
questions.explanation: The section above ======= is HEAD's version; the section below is from the branch being merged.

questions.question: What does git reset --soft HEAD~1 do?
options: Discards the last commit and all its changes
Moves the branch back one commit and leaves the changes unstaged
Moves the branch back one commit and keeps its changes staged
Creates a commit that reverses HEAD
questions.explanation: --soft moves only the branch pointer; index and working tree are untouched, so changes stay staged.

questions.question: Which command lists both local and remote-tracking branches?
questions.explanation: -a shows all branches, including remote-tracking ones.

questions.question: On branch feature, what does git rebase main do?
options: Replays feature's commits on top of main, creating new commits with new hashes
Merges main into feature with a merge commit
Deletes feature and recreates it from main
questions.explanation: Rebase re-applies commits onto a new base, rewriting them.

questions.question: After an accidental git reset --hard, which command helps you find the hash of the lost commit?
questions.explanation: The reflog records where HEAD and branches pointed, including commits no longer on any branch.

questions.question: What does git cherry-pick abc123 do?
options: Moves the branch pointer to abc123
Applies the changes introduced by abc123 as a new commit on the current branch
Marks abc123 for a later merge
questions.explanation: cherry-pick copies a commit's changes onto HEAD as a new commit.

questions.question: What does "detached HEAD" mean?
options: The current branch was deleted on the remote
HEAD points directly at a commit instead of at a branch
questions.explanation: New commits in this state belong to no branch unless you create one.

questions.question: Which command uses binary search through history to find the commit that introduced a bug?
questions.explanation: git bisect halves the range between a good and a bad commit until it finds the culprit.

questions.question: Why is git push --force-with-lease safer than git push --force?
options: It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it has moved beyond what your remote-tracking ref expects
It creates a backup branch on the remote
It works only on protected branches
questions.explanation: The lease check fails if someone else pushed commits you have not fetched, preventing you from silently discarding them.
